title: Common Table Expressions (CTE)
description: Learn how to use Common Table Expressions (CTEs) in SQL Server to build readable, modular queries.

data.text: A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary named result set that exists only during the execution of a single statement. CTEs are defined using the WITH clause and can be referenced in SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE statements.

data.title: CTE Basic Syntax
data.content: Defines a CTE and references it in the outer query.

items: Specify the expression name to which you can refer later in the query.
Optionally specify a comma-separated column list. The number of columns must match the CTE definition.
Use the AS keyword after the expression name or column list.
Define a SELECT statement whose result set populates the CTE.
Refer to the CTE in the outer query.

data.text: CTEs are preferred over subqueries because they are more readable. They are also commonly used with window functions for complex analytical queries.
The following CTE returns sales amounts by sales staff for the year 2018.

data.title: CTE for Sales Amounts by Staff
data.content: Calculates total sales by staff member for 2018 using a CTE.
data.code:
WITH cte_sales_amounts (staff, sales, year) AS (
    SELECT
        first_name + ' ' + last_name,
        SUM(quantity * list_price * (1 - discount)),
        YEAR(order_date)
    FROM
        sales.orders o
        INNER JOIN sales.order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
        INNER JOIN sales.staffs s ON s.staff_id = o.staff_id
    GROUP BY
        first_name + ' ' + last_name,
        YEAR(order_date)
)

SELECT
    staff,
    sales
FROM
    cte_sales_amounts
WHERE
    year = 2018;

data.text: This example uses a CTE to calculate the average number of sales orders in 2018 across all staff members.

data.title: CTE for Average Orders by Staff
data.content: Calculates the average number of orders per staff member using a CTE.
data.code:
WITH cte_sales AS (
    SELECT
        staff_id,
        COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM
        sales.orders
    WHERE
        YEAR(order_date) = 2018
    GROUP BY
        staff_id
)
SELECT
    AVG(order_count) AS average_orders_by_staff
FROM
    cte_sales;

data.text: Multiple CTEs in a Single Query
You can define multiple CTEs in a single WITH clause by separating them with commas. The following example uses two CTEs to return product counts and sales for each category.

data.title: Multiple CTEs Joined
data.content: Joins two CTEs to show product counts and sales per category.
data.code:
WITH cte_category_counts (
    category_id,
    category_name,
    product_count
) AS (
    SELECT
        c.category_id,
        c.category_name,
        COUNT(p.product_id)
    FROM
        production.products p
        INNER JOIN production.categories c
            ON c.category_id = p.category_id
    GROUP BY
        c.category_id,
        c.category_name
),
cte_category_sales(category_id, sales) AS (
    SELECT
        p.category_id,
        SUM(i.quantity * i.list_price * (1 - i.discount))
    FROM
        sales.order_items i
        INNER JOIN production.products p
            ON p.product_id = i.product_id
        INNER JOIN sales.orders o
            ON o.order_id = i.order_id
    WHERE
        order_status = 4
    GROUP BY
        p.category_id
)

SELECT
    c.category_id,
    c.category_name,
    c.product_count,
    s.sales
FROM
    cte_category_counts c
    INNER JOIN cte_category_sales s
        ON s.category_id = c.category_id
ORDER BY
    c.category_name;

data.title: CTE Key Points
points: CTEs make complex queries more readable by breaking them into named, reusable parts.
A CTE is defined with the WITH clause and exists only for the duration of the statement.
Multiple CTEs can be defined in a single WITH clause, separated by commas.
CTEs are preferred over subqueries for readability and maintainability.
